lesson.title: Slicing the Whole: Pie Charts and the 360 Degree Rule
lesson.summary: A pie chart turns each category's relative frequency into a slice of a circle by multiplying the proportion by 360 degrees, visually emphasizing how each part relates to the whole.
lesson.body:
A pie chart displays the distribution of a categorical variable as slices of a circle, where the size of each slice represents that category's relative frequency, its share of the whole group. Because a full circle represents 100 percent of the data, a pie chart is built directly from relative frequencies rather than raw frequencies, and it visually emphasizes how the parts relate to the whole in a way a bar graph, which emphasizes comparing category sizes to each other, does not.

To construct a pie chart, first find the relative frequency of every category, then convert each relative frequency into a slice angle by multiplying it by 360 degrees, the total number of degrees in a circle. A category representing half the data gets a slice of 0.50 times 360, which equals 180 degrees, exactly half the circle, which matches intuition and confirms the method works correctly.

Returning again to the eye color distribution, 20 students with relative frequencies brown 0.45, blue 0.30, green 0.15, and hazel 0.10, the slice angles are found by multiplying each relative frequency by 360. Brown: 0.45 times 360 equals 162 degrees. Blue: 0.30 times 360 equals 108 degrees. Green: 0.15 times 360 equals 54 degrees. Hazel: 0.10 times 360 equals 36 degrees. As a check, the four angles should add up to a full circle: 162 plus 108 plus 54 plus 36 equals 360, confirming the slices exactly fill the circle with no gap or overlap.

Pie charts only make sense for categorical variables where every individual belongs to exactly one category and the categories together account for the entire group, since the whole circle must represent 100 percent of the data with no double counting. This is also why pie charts are a poor choice for quantitative data such as test scores or heights, where dividing continuous numeric values into circle slices would obscure rather than reveal the underlying pattern, which is instead better shown with a dotplot, stemplot, or histogram.

Pie charts are most effective when there are only a handful of categories with clearly different sizes, since the human eye is better at comparing the lengths of bars than the areas of wedges, especially when several slices are close in size. For that reason, many statisticians actually prefer a bar graph over a pie chart for precise comparisons, even though pie charts remain popular for quickly communicating what share of the whole a single category represents, such as showing that brown eyes make up nearly half, 45 percent, of this particular group of students.

It is worth checking a pie chart's construction the same way you would check a frequency table or a relative frequency table. The slice angles you calculate should always sum to 360 degrees, and the relative frequencies behind them should always sum to 1. If either check fails, a category was likely left out, or a relative frequency was computed with the wrong total, the same kind of arithmetic check that mattered earlier when building the frequency and relative frequency tables a pie chart ultimately depends on.
